# Authentication API Reference

This document specifies the authentication endpoints, request and response shapes, and error codes. For conceptual guidance on choosing an auth method, see the authentication overview. For session and refresh flows, see session management.

POST /auth/login

Exchange user credentials for an access token and refresh token.

Request body:

```json
{
  "email": "user@example.com",
  "password": "..."
}
```

Successful response (200):

```json
{
  "access_token": "eyJ...",
  "refresh_token": "rt_...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 900
}
```

The `expires_in` field is the access token lifetime in seconds. The refresh token lifetime is not returned in the response and must be inferred from the configuration documentation.

POST /auth/token

Exchange an OAuth authorization code for a token. Used in the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.

Request body:

```json
{
  "grant_type": "authorization_code",
  "code": "...",
  "client_id": "...",
  "client_secret": "...",
  "redirect_uri": "..."
}
```

This endpoint is only used for OAuth flows. First-party clients should use `/auth/login` instead.

POST /auth/logout

Revoke the current access token and any associated refresh token. Requires a valid bearer token in the `Authorization` header. Returns 204 on success. Logout is idempotent — calling it with an already-revoked token returns 204, not an error.

GET /auth/me

Return the authenticated user's profile. Requires a valid bearer token. Returns 200 with the user object, or 401 if the token is invalid or expired.

Error codes

Authentication endpoints return errors in a uniform shape:

```json
{
  "error": "invalid_credentials",
  "error_description": "Email or password is incorrect.",
  "request_id": "req_..."
}
```

The error codes returned by authentication endpoints are:

`invalid_credentials` — the email or password did not match. Returned by `/auth/login` only. HTTP 401.


`token_expired` — the access token has passed its expiration time. Returned by any authenticated endpoint. HTTP 401.


`token_revoked` — the token was valid but has been explicitly revoked, typically via logout or admin action. HTTP 401.


`token_malformed` — the token does not parse as a valid JWT. HTTP 400.


`insufficient_scope` — the token is valid but lacks the scope required for the requested resource. HTTP 403.


`rate_limited` — the client has exceeded the rate limit for this endpoint. HTTP 429. Includes a `Retry-After` header.



Clients should match on `error` rather than parsing `error_description`, which is human-readable and may change between versions.

# Authentication Configuration

This document describes the deployment-time configuration for the authentication service. For endpoint specifications, see the API reference. For conceptual guidance, see the authentication overview.

Environment variables

The authentication service reads the following environment variables at startup. All variables are required unless marked optional; the service will refuse to start if a required variable is missing.

`AUTH_JWT_SIGNING_KEY` — the secret used to sign access tokens. Must be at least 32 bytes. Rotated quarterly.


`AUTH_JWT_ALGORITHM` — defaults to `HS256`. Set to `RS256` for asymmetric signing in production.


`AUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL` — access token lifetime in seconds. Default `900` (15 minutes).


`AUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL` — refresh token lifetime in seconds. Default `2592000` (30 days).


`AUTH_SESSION_INACTIVITY_TIMEOUT` — seconds of inactivity after which a session is invalidated even if the refresh token is still within its TTL. Default `86400` (24 hours).


`AUTH_DB_URL` — connection string for the auth database, which stores refresh tokens, sessions, and revocation records.


`AUTH_REDIS_URL` — connection string for the Redis instance used for the token revocation cache.


`AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` — per-IP rate limit on `/auth/login`. Default `10`.


`AUTH_OAUTH_CLIENT_REGISTRY_URL` — optional, used only when OAuth is enabled. Points to the service that maintains the registry of authorized OAuth clients.

Token TTL policy

Access tokens are short-lived (15 minutes by default) and refresh tokens are long-lived (30 days by default). The 15-minute access token TTL is a deliberate tradeoff: short enough that revocation latency is bounded without consulting the revocation cache on every request, long enough that the refresh endpoint is not hammered. Do not raise this value above 3600 (1 hour) without security review.

The refresh token TTL of 30 days reflects the maximum acceptable session duration before forced re-authentication. Reducing it below 7 days has been shown to materially hurt user experience in our deployment; raising it above 30 days requires security review.

Key rotation

JWT signing keys are rotated on a quarterly schedule. During rotation, both the previous and current keys are accepted for verification for a 24-hour overlap window, after which only the new key is accepted. Rotation is performed by updating the `AUTH_JWT_SIGNING_KEY` environment variable and triggering a rolling restart; the service reads both `AUTH_JWT_SIGNING_KEY` and `AUTH_JWT_SIGNING_KEY_PREVIOUS` during the overlap window.

API keys are not rotated on a schedule. They are rotated reactively — when an integration's keys are suspected of being compromised, or when an integration is decommissioned. API key rotation requires the integration to update its stored key; there is no overlap window for API keys.

Per-environment configuration

The default values above apply to production. Staging uses the same defaults with one exception: `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` is set to `100` in staging to permit load testing. Development environments use `AUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL=60` to make expiration scenarios easier to test, and disable rate limiting entirely by setting `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE=0`.

# Authentication Overview

This document describes the authentication model used across our services. It covers the conceptual model and decision guidance for choosing an auth strategy. For specific endpoints, see the API reference. For deployment configuration, see the configuration guide. For session and refresh flows, see session management.

Authentication vs Authorization

Authentication answers "who are you," authorization answers "what are you allowed to do." This document covers authentication only. Authorization is enforced at the resource layer via role-based access control and is described in the access control guide.

Supported authentication methods

We support three authentication methods, each suited to different use cases.

Bearer tokens are the default for first-party clients. The client obtains a token by exchanging credentials and includes the token in the `Authorization` header on subsequent requests. Bearer tokens are short-lived and paired with refresh tokens for session continuity.

API keys are used for server-to-server integrations and third-party access. API keys are long-lived, scoped to a specific integration, and revocable from the admin console. API keys do not support refresh — when an API key is rotated, the integration must be updated.

OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow is used when a third-party application needs to act on behalf of a user. The third-party redirects the user to our authorization endpoint, the user grants consent, and the third-party receives a code that is exchanged for a token.

When to use which method

Choose bearer tokens for any first-party client (web app, mobile app, internal tools). Choose API keys when a backend service needs to call our API without a user context — for example, a billing reconciliation job. Choose OAuth when you are building an integration that other developers will use to access user data.

Bearer tokens and OAuth tokens flow through the same validation path on our side; the difference is how they are obtained. API keys take a separate validation path because they do not expire and do not have an associated user session.

Failure modes

Authentication can fail for several conceptual reasons: the credential is invalid, the credential is expired, the credential is revoked, or the credential is valid but the request is malformed. The API reference enumerates the specific error codes returned for each case. Conceptually, clients should treat all authentication failures as terminal for the current request and re-authenticate before retrying — retrying with the same failed credential will not succeed.

Rate limiting is layered on top of authentication. A client whose credential is valid but whose request rate exceeds the limit will receive a rate-limit error rather than an authentication error. Clients should distinguish between the two and back off appropriately on rate-limit errors rather than re-authenticating.

# Session Management

This document describes how user sessions are established, maintained, refreshed, and terminated. It is distinct from the authentication API reference: the API reference describes the wire protocol, while this document describes the session lifecycle and the operational concerns around it.

Session model

A session is the period between a successful login and an explicit logout or session expiration. Each session is backed by a refresh token stored in the auth database, plus an access token held by the client. The session is identified server-side by a `session_id` that is embedded in the refresh token and persisted in the database.

A user may hold multiple concurrent sessions — for example, one on a desktop browser and one on a mobile device. Each session is independent: revoking one does not affect the others. The admin console exposes a per-user view of active sessions and supports targeted revocation.

Refresh flow

When an access token expires, the client exchanges the refresh token for a new access token via `POST /auth/refresh`:

```json
{
  "refresh_token": "rt_..."
}
```

The successful response includes a new access token and a new refresh token. The refresh token is rotated on every refresh. The old refresh token is invalidated as soon as the new one is issued. This is a deliberate security choice: refresh token rotation limits the blast radius of a leaked refresh token to a single use.

If a refresh request arrives with a refresh token that has already been used, the service treats this as a potential token theft scenario and revokes the entire session — not just the presented token. The client receives a `refresh_token_reused` error and must prompt the user to log in again. This policy assumes that the legitimate client will have stored the rotated refresh token; receiving the old one indicates either client misbehavior or a token leak.

Session expiration

A session ends in one of four ways:

Explicit logout. The client calls `/auth/logout` and the session is revoked immediately.


Refresh token expiration. The refresh token reaches its TTL and the next refresh attempt fails. The client must prompt the user to log in again.


Inactivity timeout. Even if the refresh token is still within its TTL, a session with no activity for the configured inactivity window is invalidated. This is enforced by tracking `last_seen_at` on the session record and rejecting refresh attempts where the gap exceeds the inactivity timeout.


Administrative revocation. A privileged user revokes the session from the admin console, or the user themselves revokes it from the security settings page.



The inactivity timeout is independent of the refresh token TTL. A session with a 30-day refresh token TTL and a 24-hour inactivity timeout will be invalidated after 24 hours of inactivity, even though the refresh token has 29 more days of nominal validity. This is intentional: the inactivity timeout protects against abandoned sessions on shared devices.

Token revocation

Revocation is implemented as a denylist in Redis, keyed by token JTI (JWT ID). When a token is revoked, its JTI is added to the denylist with a TTL equal to the token's remaining lifetime. The validation middleware checks the denylist on every request.

The denylist is the reason access tokens are short-lived: a 15-minute access token bounds the worst-case revocation latency to 15 minutes if the denylist is unavailable. If Redis is unreachable, the service fails open for access token validation — accepting tokens that may have been revoked — rather than failing closed and locking out all users. This is a deliberate availability choice and is documented as a known tradeoff.

Refresh tokens are checked against the database (not Redis) on every refresh, so refresh token revocation is immediate and does not depend on cache availability.

BEREAVEMENT LEAVE POLICY
Effective Date: January 1, 2024
Department: Human Resources
Version: 1.3

1 PURPOSE

This policy provides paid time off for employees following the death of a family member or close personal relation, recognising the need for time to grieve, attend services, and manage related affairs.

2 ELIGIBILITY

All employees are eligible from their first day of employment. There is no minimum tenure requirement. Both full-time and part-time employees are covered, with part-time entitlements pro-rated against scheduled hours.

3.1 Immediate Family

Employees may take up to 5 consecutive working days of fully paid bereavement leave following the death of an immediate family member. Immediate family is defined as: spouse or domestic partner, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, or parent-in-law.

3.2 Extended Family and Close Relations

Employees may take 1 working day of fully paid bereavement leave for the death of an extended family member or close personal relation. This includes aunts, uncles, cousins, and individuals with whom the employee had a comparably close personal relationship.

3.3 Additional Unpaid Leave

Where additional time is required, employees may request up to 10 working days of unpaid leave, subject to manager approval. Such requests will not be unreasonably refused.

4 NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS

Employees should notify their line manager as soon as reasonably possible, by phone, message, or email. Formal HR portal notification may follow within 5 working days of return. Pre-notice is not required given the unpredictable nature of bereavement.

5 SUPPORTING DOCUMENTATION

HR may request supporting documentation (such as a service notice or death certificate) only where leave exceeds 5 working days or where a pattern of usage warrants review. Documentation is not required for standard entitlements.

6 RETURN TO WORK

Employees return to their original role with no change to grade, salary, or responsibilities. Phased return arrangements may be agreed with the line manager where helpful.

7 CONTACT

For questions contact hr@company.com or speak with your HR Business Partner. The Employee Assistance Programme is also available for grief counselling support.

PARENTAL LEAVE POLICY
Effective Date: January 1, 2024
Department: Human Resources
Version: 2.1

1 PURPOSE

This policy outlines parental leave entitlements for all employees following the birth, adoption, or fostering of a child.

2 ELIGIBILITY

Employees who have completed six months of continuous employment are eligible. Both primary and secondary caregivers are covered.

3.1 Primary Caregiver

Primary caregivers receive 16 weeks of fully paid parental leave. An additional 8 weeks of unpaid leave may be taken immediately following the paid period upon written request.

3.2 Secondary Caregiver

Secondary caregivers receive 4 weeks of fully paid parental leave, to be taken within the first 12 months following the birth or placement of the child.

4 NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS

Employees must notify their line manager and HR at least 8 weeks before the intended start of leave via the HR portal.

5 RETURN TO WORK

Employees returning from parental leave are entitled to return to their original role at the same grade and salary.

6 CONTACT

For questions contact hr@company.com or speak with your HR Business Partner.

SABBATICAL LEAVE POLICY
Effective Date: January 1, 2024
Department: Human Resources
Version: 1.4

1 PURPOSE

This policy enables long-tenured employees to take an extended period of leave for personal development, study, travel, volunteer work, or rest. Sabbaticals support employee wellbeing and long-term retention.

2 ELIGIBILITY

Employees who have completed three years of continuous full-time employment are eligible to apply. Time spent on parental leave or medical leave counts toward continuous service. Time spent on prior sabbaticals does not.

3.1 Duration

Employees may take between 4 and 12 weeks of sabbatical leave. Requests longer than 12 weeks require executive approval and are considered on an exceptional basis only.

3.2 Compensation

Sabbatical leave is offered in two forms:
- Up to 4 weeks at 50% of base salary
- Up to 12 weeks fully unpaid

Employees may combine these (e.g. 4 weeks at half pay followed by 8 weeks unpaid). Benefits, including health insurance and pension contributions, continue throughout the sabbatical period.

3.3 Frequency

Eligible employees may take one sabbatical every five years. The five-year period is measured from the end date of the previous sabbatical.

4 NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS

Employees must submit a sabbatical request to their line manager and HR at least 12 weeks before the intended start of leave. Approval is subject to operational considerations including team coverage and project commitments. Requests will not be unreasonably refused but may be deferred to a later mutually agreeable date.

5 RETURN TO WORK

Employees returning from sabbatical are entitled to return to their original role at the same grade and salary. Where the original role no longer exists due to organisational change, a comparable role at the same grade will be offered.

6 CONTACT

For questions contact hr@company.com or speak with your HR Business Partner. A sabbatical planning guide is available on the HR portal.

MEDICAL LEAVE — EMPLOYEE FAQ

This page answers the most common questions about medical leave. For the full policy text, see the HR portal. For your specific situation, contact your HR Business Partner.

Q: Who is eligible for medical leave?
A: You become eligible for protected medical leave once you have completed twelve months of employment AND worked at least 1,250 hours during those twelve months. If you don't meet both conditions, you can still request unpaid leave under our discretionary leave policy, but it isn't guaranteed.

Q: How much medical leave can I take?
A: Eligible employees may take up to 12 weeks of unpaid medical leave in any rolling 12-month period. Leave may be taken in a single continuous block or, with manager and HR agreement, intermittently (e.g. for ongoing treatment).

Q: Is medical leave paid?
A: Medical leave under this policy is unpaid. However, you may be eligible for short-term disability insurance benefits during your leave, which typically replace 60% of base salary. You may also use accrued sick leave or vacation days to bridge the gap. Speak to HR before your leave starts to plan this.

Q: What documentation do I need to provide?
A: A certification from a licensed healthcare provider is required. The certification must include the date the condition began, expected duration, and a statement that you are unable to perform the essential functions of your role. HR will provide a standard certification form.

Q: How much notice do I need to give?
A: For foreseeable medical leave (e.g. scheduled surgery), 30 days written notice via the HR portal. For unforeseeable leave (e.g. sudden illness), notify your manager as soon as practicable — same day where possible, within 2 working days at the latest.

Q: What about my health insurance during medical leave?
A: Your health insurance continues uninterrupted during medical leave on the same terms as while actively working. The company continues its contribution; you continue yours, typically by automatic deduction from any short-term disability payments or by direct payment to HR.

Q: Will my job be there when I come back?
A: Yes. Upon return from medical leave you are entitled to return to your original role at the same grade and salary. If your original role is genuinely no longer available due to circumstances unrelated to your leave, a comparable role will be offered.

Q: Can my medical leave be extended beyond 12 weeks?
A: Extensions beyond 12 weeks fall outside this policy and are handled case-by-case, often as a reasonable accommodation under disability law. Contact HR before your initial 12 weeks ends to discuss options.

Q: How does medical leave interact with parental leave?
A: Pregnancy-related medical leave (e.g. recovery from childbirth) is treated as medical leave. Parental leave for bonding with a new child is separate and runs under the parental leave policy. The two can be taken consecutively.

For questions not covered here, contact hr@company.com.

WELLNESS BENEFITS — EMPLOYEE FAQ

This page covers the wellness benefits available to employees. These are separate from medical leave (see medical leave FAQ) and from health insurance (see your benefits enrollment portal).

Q: Who is eligible for wellness benefits?
A: All full-time employees are eligible from their first day of employment. Part-time employees scheduled for 20 or more hours per week are eligible on a pro-rated basis. Contractors and interns are not covered under this programme.

Q: What's covered under the wellness stipend?
A: Each eligible employee receives an annual wellness stipend of $1,200, reimbursable against qualifying expenses. Qualifying expenses include: gym and fitness studio memberships, fitness equipment for home use up to $400, mental health apps and therapy copays, nutrition counselling, sleep aids and ergonomic equipment, and wellness retreats.

Q: What is NOT covered?
A: The stipend does not cover: cosmetic procedures, supplements or vitamins, weight-loss medications, recreational equipment unrelated to fitness (e.g. ski passes), or expenses already covered by health insurance.

Q: How do I claim reimbursement?
A: Submit receipts via the wellness portal within 60 days of the expense. Reimbursement is processed in the next payroll cycle following approval. Claims older than 60 days are not accepted except in documented exceptional circumstances.

Q: Does the stipend roll over year to year?
A: No. The wellness stipend resets on January 1 each year. Unused amounts are not paid out and do not carry forward. Plan your claims accordingly.

Q: Is the Employee Assistance Programme part of this?
A: The Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) is separate and free at point of use. It provides confidential short-term counselling, legal advice, and financial guidance. EAP usage does not draw from your wellness stipend. Contact the EAP directly via the number on the back of your employee ID card.

Q: Are mental health benefits covered?
A: Yes, in three ways: (1) therapy copays from your health insurance can be reimbursed via the wellness stipend; (2) standalone mental health apps (e.g. meditation, CBT-based) are covered up to the stipend limit; (3) the EAP provides up to 8 free counselling sessions per issue per year, separate from the stipend.

Q: How does this differ from medical leave?
A: Wellness benefits are an ongoing benefit while you are actively working. Medical leave is time off when you cannot work due to a health condition. They are unrelated programmes with different eligibility rules and entitlements.

Q: Is the stipend taxable?
A: Reimbursements through the wellness stipend are generally treated as taxable income and appear on your annual wage statement. Consult a tax advisor for your specific situation. The company does not provide tax advice.

For questions not covered here, contact hr@company.com.

TICKET ID: SUP-1042
DATE: 2024-02-14
CATEGORY: authentication
STATUS: resolved
PRIORITY: high

TITLE: Users unable to login after password reset

DESCRIPTION:
Multiple users reported being unable to log in after using the password reset flow. The login endpoint returns 401 even with correct new credentials.

INVESTIGATION:
The password reset flow was writing the new password hash to the read replica instead of the primary database due to a misconfigured connection string introduced in v1.8.2. Login reads from primary, so the new hash was never visible to the login check.

ROOT CAUSE:
Environment variable AUTH_DB_WRITE_URL was accidentally set to the read replica URL in the v1.8.2 Helm chart. The variable was renamed from DB_PRIMARY_URL in v1.8.0 but the Helm chart was not updated consistently.

RESOLUTION:
Rolled back Helm chart to v1.8.1 values. Issued hotfix in v1.8.3 with correct environment variable. Affected users were sent a new password reset email. Total affected users: 47.

PREVENTION:
Added integration test verifying password reset flow end to end. Added Helm chart CI linting to validate required environment variables are present.

TICKET ID: SUP-1108
DATE: 2024-04-22
CATEGORY: authentication
STATUS: resolved
PRIORITY: high

TITLE: Intermittent login failures following v2.1.0 deploy

DESCRIPTION:
Following the v2.1.0 production deploy, approximately 30% of login attempts began failing with HTTP 401 responses. Users who were already logged in remained authenticated, but new login attempts and token refresh attempts failed inconsistently. Failures appeared to correlate with which pod served the request.

INVESTIGATION:
Initial suspicion was a database issue similar to SUP-1042, but the password store was confirmed correct and the login endpoint was reading from the primary database. Examination of pod logs showed JWT signature validation failures, specifically "kid not found in keyring" errors. The signing key had been rotated as part of v2.1.0, but pods deployed before the rotation completed had cached the previous keyring at startup and never refreshed it.

ROOT CAUSE:
The JWT signing keyring is loaded once at pod startup and held in memory. Key rotation publishes new keys to the keyring service but does not signal running pods to refresh. Pods deployed between the rotation start and rotation completion ended up with a partial keyring containing only the old key. When a token signed with the new key reached an old-keyring pod, validation failed.

RESOLUTION:
Rolling restart of the affected deployment forced all pods to reload the keyring from scratch, picking up both old and new keys. Login success rate returned to baseline within 4 minutes of restart completion.

PREVENTION:
Added a periodic keyring refresh (every 5 minutes) so pods pick up rotations without requiring restart. Added a startup readiness check that fails the pod if the keyring contains fewer than the expected number of active keys. Updated the deploy runbook to require a rolling restart following any signing key rotation until the periodic refresh has been verified in production for 30 days.

TICKET ID: SUP-1156
DATE: 2024-06-08
CATEGORY: infrastructure
STATUS: resolved
PRIORITY: medium

TITLE: Login failures concentrated among subset of users

DESCRIPTION:
Customer support escalated reports of approximately 200 users unable to log in over a 6-hour period. Affected users could enter credentials and receive a successful authentication response, but were redirected back to the login page on the next request. The session appeared to be lost immediately after creation. The same user could sometimes log in successfully on retry. Users not in the affected set reported no issues.

INVESTIGATION:
Authentication itself was functioning correctly — credentials validated, tokens issued, password store healthy. The issue was traced to session storage. Sessions are stored in Redis sharded by user ID hash. One Redis shard (shard-3 of 8) was running at 98% memory utilisation and had begun evicting keys under maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru. Sessions for users hashing to shard-3 were being evicted within seconds of creation, causing the immediate logout behaviour.

ROOT CAUSE:
Shard-3 had grown disproportionately due to a bug in the user-ID hash function introduced in a refactor three months prior. The hash was meant to distribute uniformly across 8 shards but produced a distribution skewed roughly 3:1 toward shard-3. The imbalance went unnoticed because total Redis capacity remained sufficient until a recent user growth spike pushed shard-3 specifically over its limit.

RESOLUTION:
Immediate mitigation: increased shard-3 memory allocation by 4x to halt evictions. Permanent fix: corrected the hash function and ran a re-sharding job to redistribute existing session keys evenly across all 8 shards. The re-sharding ran during a low-traffic window and forced affected users to re-authenticate once.

PREVENTION:
Added per-shard memory utilisation alerts at 75% and 90% thresholds. Added a daily job that reports shard distribution skew and pages on-call if any shard holds more than 1.5x the median. Added an integration test verifying the hash function produces uniform distribution across shard counts of 4, 8, and 16.

TICKET ID: SUP-1203
DATE: 2024-08-15
CATEGORY: email-delivery
STATUS: resolved
PRIORITY: medium

TITLE: Password reset emails not delivered to subset of users

DESCRIPTION:
Users reported requesting a password reset and never receiving the reset email. The application showed the standard "if an account exists, an email has been sent" confirmation, but no email arrived in the user's inbox or spam folder. Affected users were able to log in normally if they remembered their existing password, ruling out account state issues. The password reset flow itself completed successfully on the backend; only email delivery failed.

INVESTIGATION:
Backend logs showed password reset requests reaching the email service and being submitted to AWS SES. SES responses indicated successful submission for some emails but ThrottlingException errors for others, particularly during peak hours. The SES sending quota was being hit for our region, and submissions over the per-second send rate were rejected. Rejected submissions were logged but not retried.

ROOT CAUSE:
Two issues compounded: (1) our SES sending rate had been provisioned for an earlier user base size and not increased as the user base grew; (2) the email service had no retry logic for ThrottlingException, so any rate-limited email was silently dropped. The combination meant that during peak hours roughly 8% of password reset emails were never sent.

RESOLUTION:
Immediate mitigation: requested an SES quota increase from AWS, approved within 4 hours. Added exponential-backoff retry logic to the email service for ThrottlingException specifically (other SES errors are not retried). Affected users from the prior 48 hours were proactively sent a new password reset email outside peak hours.

PREVENTION:
Added monitoring for SES throttling errors with alerting at any rate above 0.1% of email volume. Added a quarterly review of SES sending quotas against projected user growth. Made retry logic the default for all transient SES errors, with a maximum of 3 attempts and dead-letter logging for emails that exhaust retries.

AUTHENTICATION TROUBLESHOOTING RUNBOOK
Owner: Platform Team
Last Reviewed: 2024-09-01

This runbook is the first stop for on-call engineers responding to authentication-related incidents. Work through the symptom sections in order. Each section lists what to check, what indicates that path, and where to escalate or reference past incidents.

SYMPTOM 1: All users see HTTP 401 on login
This is a total auth outage. Highest priority.
Check first: is the auth service itself running? Hit /health on the auth service directly. If down, escalate to Platform on-call immediately.
If healthy: check the password store database connection. Look for "connection refused" or "read-only" errors in auth service logs. A common past cause was the password store write URL pointing at a read replica (see SUP-1042).
If database is healthy: check the JWT signing keyring. Look for "kid not found" errors in logs. Recent key rotations are the usual cause.

SYMPTOM 2: Some users can log in, others cannot
This pattern indicates a partial failure rather than a service outage.
Check first: is the failure correlated with which pod served the request? Aggregate failure logs by pod ID. If one pod or one deployment shows disproportionate failures, the keyring may be stale on that subset (see SUP-1108). Mitigation: rolling restart of the affected deployment.
If pod distribution looks uniform: check whether the failure correlates with user ID. Pull a sample of failing user IDs and check their session storage shard. If failing users cluster on one Redis shard, you have a session storage problem (see SUP-1156).
If neither pod nor shard correlates: check for IP-based rate limiting or geo-blocking that may have been recently changed.

SYMPTOM 3: Login succeeds but session is immediately lost
The user authenticates, gets redirected to the app, and is bounced back to the login page on the next request.
This is almost always session storage. Check Redis health, especially memory utilisation and eviction counters. A shard at >90% memory under allkeys-lru policy will evict sessions within seconds (see SUP-1156).
Less common: check for cookie domain mismatches if the issue started after a recent frontend deploy. The session cookie may be being set on the wrong domain.

SYMPTOM 4: Password reset flow appears broken
Distinguish two sub-cases before investigating.
Sub-case A: user submits reset request, receives email, clicks link, enters new password, but cannot log in with the new password. This is the reset-write path. Check that the new password hash is being written to the primary database, not a replica (see SUP-1042). Also check that the login endpoint reads from the same database the reset writes to.
Sub-case B: user submits reset request, never receives email. This is the email delivery path, not the auth path. Check SES sending logs for ThrottlingException or other delivery errors (see SUP-1203). Auth service logs will show the reset request as successful even when email delivery failed.

SYMPTOM 5: Token refresh fails but initial login works
Check JWT signing keyring first; this is usually the same root cause as Symptom 1 sub-cases (see SUP-1108). Refresh tokens are validated against the same keyring as access tokens.

ESCALATION
If none of the above paths identifies the cause within 30 minutes, page Platform on-call. Capture: failure rate, affected user IDs (sample), pod distribution of failures, recent deploys, recent infra changes, and Redis shard memory state. Attach this to the incident channel before escalating.
